title: Which teachers of punishment change lives
source_text: Εἶτ᾿ οὐκ οἶδ᾿ ὅπως ὁ Κέλσος τὴν προθυμίαν τῶν μέχρι θανάτου ἀγωνιζομένων ὑπὲρ τοῦ μὴ ἐξομόσασθαι χριστιανιασμὸν παρατιθέμενος ἐπιφέρει ὡσπερεὶ ἐξισῶν τὰ ἡμέτερα τοῖς ὑπὸ τῶν τελεστῶν καὶ μυσταγωγῶν λεγομένοις καί φησι· μάλιστα μὲν, ὦ βέλτιστε, ὥσπερ σὺ κολάσεις αἰωνίους νομίζεις, οὕτως καὶ οἱ τῶν ἱερῶν ἐκείνων ἐξηγηταὶ τελεσταί τε καὶ μυσταγωγοί· ἃς σὺ μὲν τοῖς ἄλλοις ἀπειλεῖς, ἐκεῖνοι δὲ σοί. πότερα γὰρ αὐτῶν ἀληθέστερα ἢ ἐπικρατέστερα, ἔξεστι σκοπεῖν. λόγῳ μὲν γὰρ ἐξ ἴσου περὶ τῶν σφετέρων σφίσιν ἑκάτεροι διαβεβαιοῦσθε· τεκμηρίων δὲ εἰ δέοι. πολλὰ ἐκεῖνοι καὶ ἐναργῆ δεικνύουσιν ἔργα τε δαιμονίων τινῶν δυνάμεων καὶ χρηστηρίων καὶ ἐκ παντοδαπῶν μαντείων προκομίζοντες. οὐκοῦν διὰ τούτων τὰς αἰωνίους κολάσεις ἐπ᾿ ἴσης βούλεται καὶ ἡμᾶς λέγειν καὶ τοὺς τελεστὰς καὶ ἐξετάζειν, ὁπότεροι μᾶλλον ἀληθεύουσιν. εἴποιμι δ᾿ ἂν ἀληθεύειν τοὺς δυνηθέντας διαθεῖναι τοὺς ἀκροατὰς τῶν λεγομένων οὕτως βιοῦντας, ὡς τούτων οὕτως ἐχόντων. διατίθενται Ἰουδαῖοι καὶ Χριστιανοὶ περὶ τοῦ ὑπ᾿ αὐτῶν καλουμένου μέλλοντος αἰῶνος καὶ τῶν ἐν αὐτῷ γερῶν μὲν ἐπὶ τοὺς δικαίους κολάσεων δὲ ἐπὶ τοὺς ἁμαρτωλούς. δεικνύτω οὖν καὶ Κέλσος ἢ ὁ βουλόμενος, τίνες διετέθησαν περὶ αἰωνίων κολάσεων ὑπὸ τῶν τελεστῶν καὶ μυσταγωγῶν. εἰκὸς γάρ ἐστι τὸ βούλημα τοῦ πατρὸς τῶν λεγομένων εἶναι οὐ τὸ ἀφοσιοῦσθαι μόνον καὶ εἰπεῖν περὶ κολάσεων ἀλλὰ τὸ διαθεῖναι τοὺς ἀκούοντας πρὸς τὸ ὅση δύναμις φυλάξασθαι τὰ τῶν κολάσεων αἴτια αὐτοὺς ἐργάσασθαι. ἀλλὰ καὶ αἱ προφητεῖαι τοῖς μὴ παρέργως ἐντυγχάνουσι τῇ ἐν αὐταῖς προγνώσει ἱκαναί μοι εἶναι δοκοῦσι πρὸς τὸ πεῖσαι τὸν συνετῶς ἅμα καὶ εὐγνωμόνως ἀναγινώσκοντα ὅτι θεοῦ πνεῦμα ἦν ἐν τοῖς ἀνδράσιν ἐκείνοις· αἷς οὐδὲν τῶν δεικνυμένων ἔργων δαιμονίων οὐδὲ τῶν ἐκ χρηστηρίων δυνάμεων οὐδὲ τῶν μαντειῶν κἂν ἐπὶ ποσὸν παραβάλλεσθαι δύναται.
pass_a_gloss: Then I do not know how Celsus, setting forth (παρατιθέμενος) the eagerness (προθυμία) of those contending (ἀγωνιζομένων) until death so as not to forswear (ἐξομόσασθαι) Christianity, adds, as if equating (ἐξισῶν) ours with the things said by the initiators (τελεστῶν) and mystagogues (μυσταγωγῶν), and says: Most of all, best one, as you believe (νομίζεις) eternal punishments (κολάσεις αἰωνίους), so also the interpreters (ἐξηγηταί) of those sacred rites (ἱερῶν), initiators and mystagogues; which you threaten (ἀπειλεῖς) to others, they to you. Which of them is truer or more prevailing (ἐπικρατέστερα) one may examine (σκοπεῖν). For in word each equally affirms (διαβεβαιοῦσθε) about their own; but if proofs (τεκμηρίων) were needed, they show many and clear (ἐναργῆ), bringing forward works of certain demonic powers (δαιμονίων δυνάμεων) and of oracles (χρηστηρίων) and from all sorts of divinations (μαντείων). — So through these he wishes us and the initiators equally to speak of eternal punishments and to examine which speak more truly (ἀληθεύουσιν). I would say those speak truly who were able to dispose (διαθεῖναι) the hearers to live (βιοῦντας) as though these things are so. Jews and Christians are disposed about what they call the coming age (μέλλοντος αἰῶνος) and the rewards (γερῶν) in it for the just and punishments for sinners. Let Celsus or whoever wishes show who were disposed about eternal punishments by the initiators and mystagogues. For likely the intention (βούλημα) of the father (πατρός) of the things said is not only to discharge a formality (ἀφοσιοῦσθαι) and speak of punishments, but to dispose the hearers, as far as power allows, to guard against (φυλάξασθαι) doing the causes (αἴτια) of punishments. But also the prophecies (προφητεῖαι), to those reading not carelessly (μὴ παρέργως), by the foreknowledge (πρόγνωσις) in them seem to me sufficient (ἱκαναί) to persuade the one reading intelligently and fairly (συνετῶς, εὐγνωμόνως) that the Spirit of God (θεοῦ πνεῦμα) was in those men; with which none of the displayed demonic works nor of the powers from oracles nor of divinations can be compared (παραβάλλεσθαι) even to a small degree (ἐπὶ ποσόν).
pass_b_english: Then, I do not know how, Celsus, after bringing forward the zeal of those who contend even to death rather than forswear Christianity, goes on as though putting our teachings on a level with what the initiators and mystagogues say, and he says: “Indeed, my good sir, just as you believe in eternal punishments, so too do the interpreters of those sacred rites, the initiators and mystagogues. You threaten others with them, and they threaten you. For one may well examine which of the two are truer or more powerful. As far as words go, you and they alike affirm your own claims with equal confidence; but if proofs were needed, they display many clear ones, bringing forward the works of certain demonic powers and of oracles, and proofs drawn from divinations of every kind.”

By this, then, he would have it that we and the initiators alike speak of eternal punishments, and he wants to inquire which of the two speak more truly. I would say that those speak the truth who have been able to bring their hearers to live as men convinced that these things are so. Jews and Christians are so convinced about what they call the age to come, and about the rewards in it for the righteous and the punishments for sinners. Let Celsus, then, or anyone who wishes, show who have been brought to such conviction about eternal punishments by the initiators and mystagogues. For it is likely that the aim of anyone who fathers such teachings is not merely to discharge a formality by speaking about punishments, but to bring his hearers, as far as lies in their power, to guard against doing the things that lead to punishment.

Moreover, to those who read them with care, the prophecies seem to me enough, by the foreknowledge they contain, to persuade anyone who reads with understanding and fairness that the Spirit of God was in those men. With these prophecies none of the demonic works that are displayed, none of the powers that come from oracles, and none of the divinations can be compared in the slightest degree.

choices.choice: Celsus’s words run from ‘Indeed, my good sir’ to ‘divinations of every kind’. μάλιστα μέν opening the quotation is taken as an affirming ‘Indeed’ (it may also mean ‘Above all’). λόγῳ μὲν ... ἑκάτεροι διαβεβαιοῦσθε: the second-person plural takes in both parties (‘you and they alike’). δαιμονίων δυνάμεων: Celsus means daemonic (supernatural) powers without blame; ‘demonic’ is kept, as elsewhere in this Book, so that Origen’s reply can echo the same words. ‘The father of these teachings’ (πατὴρ τῶν λεγομένων) means the originator of a doctrine, not God, so it stays lowercase; rendered ‘anyone who fathers such teachings’ because Origen states a general rule. ‘The age to come’ (μέλλων αἰών) is common New Testament language (Matthew 12:32; Hebrews 6:5) but Origen presents it as Jewish and Christian usage, not a quotation, so it is not cited inline. The claim that the Spirit of God was in the prophets may recall 2 Peter 1:21 or 1 Peter 1:11; not a clear allusion, left uncited.
Restored γάρ in Celsus's 'For one may well examine which of the two...'
'in word each of you affirms your own teachings' -> 'As far as words go, you and they alike affirm your own claims' (ἑκάτεροι with second-person plural covers both parties; stiff Greek order removed)
'and from divinations of every kind' -> 'and proofs drawn from divinations of every kind' (the object τεκμήρια supplied from the clause, keeps the parallel clear)
'he wants us and the initiators alike to be said to teach ... and wants it examined' -> 'he would have it that we and the initiators alike speak of ... and he wants to inquire' (λέγειν, ἐξετάζειν)
'have been brought to such conviction' -> 'are so convinced' for present διατίθενται
'the aim of the father of these teachings was' -> 'the aim of anyone who fathers such teachings is' (εἰκός ἐστι ... εἶναι, present general statement)

choices.choice: 8.48: Celsus's δαιμονίων δυνάμεων is a neutral word for him (supernatural powers). It is kept as 'demonic' to match the rest of Book 8 and so Origen's reply can echo it, with a translator note. The owner may prefer 'daemonic' for Celsus's own words across the whole work.
